title: High-Wind and Rooftop Cover Installation
excerpt: Cover on the ground after the first storm? Rooftops and open yards need tie-downs to curb anchors, a crowned top for drainage, and a post-storm re-tension check.

content.heading: Problem: Drawcord Alone on a Rooftop
content.body: Residential wall mounts often survive with a hem drawcord. Rooftops and open equipment yards see sustained 25+ mph gusts — wind gets under a loose hem and the cover becomes a sail. Bungee cords stretch and detach; the cover ends up on a lower roof or in the yard.

content.heading: Solution: Minimum Rooftop Install
content.body: After standard drape and hem secure, add mechanical tie-downs.
bullets: Ratchet straps or UV-rated cable ties to curb anchors or frame legs — not bungee alone
Reinforced top panel if rain or snow load is expected
Crown the top slightly with strap tension so water runs to edges, not into louvers
Route hem so runoff drains away from the cabinet opening, not into the pan area

content.heading: After the First Storm
content.body: Walk the roof and re-tension every strap. Flutter at corners means the cover shifted — fix it before the next front, not after you find it on the ground.

title: Top Benefits of Using a Cooler Cover
excerpt: Fix winter drafts, skip spring rust cleanup, and avoid pad replacement — a cover pays for itself the first season you would have otherwise serviced the pan.

content.heading: Problem: Cold Rooms After You Shut Down
content.body: An uncovered cooler is an open duct to the outside. Cold air drafts through the intakes, through the cabinet, and into your house all winter. Sealing the intakes with a fitted cover stops that path — many homeowners notice warmer rooms within the first week.

content.heading: Problem: Expensive Spring Startup
content.body: Rain, debris, and pests in an open cabinet drive most off-season repair bills.
bullets: Rust in the water pan and hardware — often needs replacement, not just cleaning
Wasps and rodents nesting inside — removal before first run
UV-cracked louvers and dried-out pads — premature wear
Half a day of scrubbing before you can turn the unit on

title: Bulk vs Small Batch Cooler Cover Orders
excerpt: Need 5 units tomorrow but bulk pricing kicks in at 25? Prototype first, then bulk when the pattern is approved — we quote both tiers near the crossover.

content.heading: Problem: Wrong Order Tier Wastes Money or Time
content.body: Bulk before prototype approval → remakes at scale. Small batch when you need 40 identical units → per-unit cost stays high. Match tier to pattern certainty and quantity.

content.heading: Choose Small Batch When
bullets: First time covering this cabinet model — pattern not yet approved
Quantity under ~25, or mixed sizes in low counts
Tight deadline on a handful of units before shutdown season

content.heading: Choose Bulk When
bullets: Prototype fit and openings approved
25+ units, same material spec and pattern ID
Logo setup should amortize across the run

title: Common Cooler Cover Sizing Mistakes
excerpt: Hem binds on casters, corners gape, or you ordered pad width instead of cabinet size — five measurement errors that cause most returns.

content.heading: Problem: Cover Arrived "Correct Size" But Won't Fit
content.body: Returns usually trace back to how the unit was measured — not the chart. Pad dimensions, inside cabinet depth, and catalog "unit size" labels are all smaller than the outside outline the cover must wrap.

content.heading: Five Mistakes → Fix
bullets: Measured pad area, not outside cabinet → remeasure widest W×D×H
Forgot casters (add 3–6") → include floor-to-highest-point height
Between chart rows and sized down → always size up; drawcord takes slack
Side-draft cover on down-draft unit (or reverse) → match profile to intake location
One size for three models → one row per model in your dimension table

content.heading: Quick Fit Check Before You Call It Done
bullets: Hem sits below lowest louver — not above casters
No fabric stretched drum-tight over hose ports
All intake panels sealed with no visible gaps at corners
Drawcord or strap engaged under frame, not floating at mid-panel

title: Advanced Installation & Care Topics
excerpt: Cover blew off, water pooling on top, or hem won't fit? Standard install is in the resource guide — these articles fix wind, fit, and field failures.

content.heading: First Time? Start With the Resource Guide
content.body: Drape cover, secure hem, add tie-downs if exposed — the step-by-step sequence is on our installation page. Come back here when something still fails after following those steps.

content.heading: Problem → Which Article
bullets: Cover blew off rooftop or open yard → high-wind install
Water pools, mold smell, hem gaps → troubleshooting table
Cover too tight, corners open, wrong draft type → sizing mistakes

title: Cooler Cover Materials & Performance Guide
excerpt: Fabric faded in one season, water wicking through seams, or mesh used for winter? Pick material by how the unit fails in your storage conditions — not by lowest price.

content.heading: Problem: Cover Failed Early — Why?
content.body: Match the failure mode to the fabric fix.
bullets: Faded, brittle, torn at caster rub points → UV/denier issue (see UV article)
Water inside cabinet after rain → wrong waterproof rating (see waterproof article)
Cold drafts with cover on → mesh or vented used for winter (see vented vs closed)
Condensation in freezing yard after proper drain → consider insulated liner

content.heading: Default Picks by Condition
bullets: Dry Southwest winter shutdown → 600D PU polyester
Standing water on top, coastal, or heavy snow → vinyl-coated polyester
Idle in summer dust, unit not winterized → mesh (in-season only)

title: Custom Cooler Covers: Complete Customization Guide
excerpt: Stock cover rips on casters, gaps at hose ports, or a fleet with three different models? Custom patterns fix fit once — then reorder by pattern ID.

content.heading: When Stock Covers Fail
content.body: If any of these sound familiar, custom is faster than fighting returns.
bullets: Hem binds on casters or hose ports — fabric stretched, wind gets under the edge
Control panel or fill cap forces you to leave a corner open
Three cabinet models in one yard — one "42-inch" size fits none of them well
Procurement needs the same material code and color on every PO

content.heading: What to Send for an Accurate Quote
content.body: Four inputs — missing any one slows approval or causes a remake.
bullets: Outside W×D×H per model (include casters and protrusions)
Material + color for your climate (see materials article)
Opening locations — photos with a tape measure in frame
Quantity, timeline, and logo file if branding is required

content.heading: Typical Workflow
bullets: 1. Submit dimensions + photos → quote with material options
2. Prototype one unit → field test fit and openings
3. Approve pattern → bulk or small-batch production
4. Reorders use stored pattern ID — no remeasure unless the cabinet changes

title: Custom Cover Materials: What to Specify
excerpt: Fabric failed in one season, or covers sit in a wet yard? Pick 600D PU, vinyl, mesh, or insulated based on how the unit is stored — not catalog default.

content.heading: Problem: Wrong Fabric for Storage Conditions
content.body: Cheap fabric fades and tears at caster contact points in one Southwest summer. Mesh used as a winter cover lets cold air straight through. Spec the fabric to your worst storage condition, not average weather.

content.heading: Solution: Pick by Condition
bullets: Dry equipment yard, winter shutdown → 600D polyester + PU coating (default)
Rain/snow load on top, coastal or rooftop → vinyl-coated polyester
Idle in summer dust, unit still needs airflow → mesh (in-season only)
Freezing yard, months outdoors after full drain/dry → insulated liner option

content.heading: Lock the Spec for Reorders
content.body: Record material code and color on the PO template. Mixed specs across a fleet means some units fail early while others last — procurement cannot troubleshoot fabric in the field.

title: Custom Cover Sizes: How to Submit Dimensions
excerpt: Cover too tight at the hem or gaps at corners? You measured pad width or forgot casters. Submit outside cabinet dimensions — one row per model.

content.heading: Problem: Returns From Bad Measurements
content.body: Pad width is smaller than the cabinet. Casters add 3–6 inches stock charts ignore. Averaging three models into one size fits none of them. Custom only works if dimensions reflect the real outside outline.

content.heading: Solution: Measure Outside at Widest Points
bullets: Width — widest face, including side handles or panel bumps
Depth — include hose ports or panels that stick out past the frame
Height — floor to highest point, casters included
One spreadsheet row per model number — never one "average" row for a mixed fleet

content.heading: Between Chart Sizes?
content.body: If you land between stock chart rows, size up — a slightly loose hem with a drawcord fits; a tight cover tears at corners and rides up in wind.

title: Custom Opening Designs for Cooler Covers
excerpt: Stretched fabric over a hose port, or a flap that won't stay closed in wind? Openings must align with real hardware — send photos and dimensions.

content.heading: Problem: Cover Fights the Hardware
content.body: Without cutouts, crews stretch fabric over hose fittings or leave the hem open to reach the panel. Both fail — stretched fabric tears; open hems let wind under the cover.

content.heading: Solution: Match Opening to Use Case
bullets: Hose connection — reinforced grommet or zip panel at port height
Control panel — Velcro flap for occasional winter access without removing the cover
Fill cap — small zip or snap closure; mark left/right in photos
Include tape measure in photos — we place openings from your dimensions, not guesses

content.heading: Prototype First
content.body: First order for a new model: approve one unit before fleet qty. Field-test zippers and flap placement — moving an opening after 40 covers are cut is expensive.

title: Evaporative Cooler Covers: Types, Fit & Buying Guide
excerpt: Compare side-draft, down-draft, portable, and custom evaporative cooler covers by size, fabric, tie-down, and off-season use.

content.heading: Quick Buying Guide
content.body: Start with the cooler profile, then match the outside dimensions and exposure. Retail covers commonly run from about $14 for small portable units to $72+ for large rooftop or heavy-duty models; custom pricing depends on size, fabric, openings, quantity, and logo requirements.
bullets: Side-draft unit → tall cover that wraps every side intake
Down-draft rooftop unit → wide, lower profile with reinforced top and tie-downs
Portable cooler → model-specific lightweight cover with a drawcord
Pipes, disconnect boxes, or unusual proportions → made-to-measure pattern

content.heading: Which Problem Are You Fixing?
content.body: Most cover orders start with one of these — match your situation to the right next step.
bullets: Rooms feel colder after shutdown → you need a cover that seals intake panels (see benefits + winterizing)
Rust, mold, or wasps every spring → drain/dry first, then cover (winterizing checklist)
Cover won't fit or blows off → wrong type or size; remeasure outside W×D×H
Not sure what a cover even does → start with what-is article below

content.heading: Three Decisions Before You Order
content.body: Get these right and most returns disappear.
bullets: Cooler type — side draft, down draft, rooftop, or window (profile must match intakes)
Outside size — widest W×D×H including casters; between chart rows, size up
Fabric — 600D PU for dry winters; vinyl if rain pools on the unit; mesh never for winter

content.heading: Articles in This Guide
content.body: Each article solves one decision. Full install and maintenance steps live on our resource pages.
bullets: What is a cooler cover? — do you actually need one?
Top benefits — draft blocking and spring startup
Winterizing — shutdown order before the cover goes on

title: Insulated Swamp Cooler Covers
excerpt: Condensation inside a covered unit in a freezing yard? Insulation helps only after full drain/dry — it does not fix a wet pan or skipped shutdown.

content.heading: Problem: Condensation in Cold Storage
content.body: Units sit in freezing equipment yards for months. Temperature swings inside a sealed cover can produce condensation on metal surfaces — even when the unit was shut down correctly.

content.heading: Solution: Insulated Liner After Proper Shutdown
content.body: Insulation reduces temperature swing inside a dry, covered cabinet. Prerequisites still apply.
bullets: Pan drained and dry — insulation does not stop mold from a wet shutdown
Pads replaced or fully dried before cover goes on
Use only after complete winterizing — see checklist

content.heading: When Insulation Will Not Help
bullets: Cover put on while pan still had water → mold regardless of liner
Unit run with cover installed → overheating risk
Substitute for drain/dry steps → always fails by spring

title: Logo Printing on Cooler Covers
excerpt: Fleet units look identical in the yard? Screen print for volume; heat transfer for mixed sizes. One setup fee — art file stored for reorders.

content.heading: Problem: Unmarked Fleet Covers
content.body: Rental and event yards lose track of which covers belong to which client. Logo on the side panel at eye height solves identification and doubles as brand visibility on site.

content.heading: Solution: Method by Quantity
bullets: 25+ identical covers, 1–2 colors → screen print (lowest per-unit cost at volume)
Mixed sizes or full-color logo → heat transfer
Submit vector art (AI/EPS/SVG); high-res PNG works if lines are clean
Setup fee applies once — stored screens/files used on reorders

content.heading: Before Production Runs
content.body: We confirm placement on the prototype cover. Side panel placement avoids hem and opening conflict — moving logo after bulk cut is not practical.

title: Mesh Swamp Cooler Covers
excerpt: Pads clogging with yard dust on idle summer units? Mesh keeps debris off while air flows. It will not stop winter drafts, rain, or pests — use solid fabric for shutdown.

content.heading: Problem: Dust on Idle Units During Cooling Season
content.body: Portable units sit in gravel yards between jobs. Wind-blown dust loads pads on idle coolers — startup airflow drops and pads need early replacement. Mesh blocks debris while allowing air through.

content.heading: Solution: Mesh for In-Season Idle Only
bullets: Use when the unit is off but not winterized — still needs airflow
Keeps leaves and dust off pads without trapping heat like solid fabric
Swap to solid winter cover at shutdown — mesh is not a winter product

content.heading: Do Not Use Mesh When
bullets: Winter shutdown — cold air passes straight through mesh
Rain protection needed — water penetrates openly
Pest blocking — mesh openings are too large for wasps and rodents

title: Down Draft Swamp Cooler Covers
excerpt: Rain sitting on top of the unit, or top intake still open? Down-draft cabinets need a wide, low cover with a reinforced top — sides alone are not enough.

content.heading: Problem: Water Pools or Top Intake Exposed
content.body: Down-draft units pull air through the top deck. Sides are mostly solid. A side-draft cover leaves the primary intake open and may sag in the middle — rainwater pools instead of running off.

content.heading: Solution: Down-Draft Profile + Drainage
bullets: Wide, low cover shape — top panel is the critical seal
Reinforced top for rain and snow load in open yards
Tighten straps so the top crowns slightly — water runs to edges, not into louvers
Confirm outlet duct clearance before ordering — depth must clear roof connections

content.heading: Open Yard Storage
content.body: Add tie-downs on exposed sites. Re-tension after the first storm — a sagging top is the main cause of pooled water and interior rust.

title: Side Draft Swamp Cooler Covers
excerpt: Cold air still coming in after covering? Side louvers are probably open — you need a tall cover that wraps the intake panels, not a down-draft top-only profile.

content.heading: Problem: Side Intakes Still Open
content.body: Side-draft portables pull air through large louvers on the left and right faces. A cover that only seals the top leaves both intakes exposed — drafts and debris get in exactly where you thought you were protected.

content.heading: Solution: Identify and Wrap Side Draft
content.body: Large intake louvers on left/right; outlet on top or front.
bullets: Use a side-draft profile — tall enough to wrap both intake faces
Hem below the lowest louver edge, not mid-panel
Route drawcord or strap under the caster frame so wind cannot lift the hem
Do not substitute a down-draft cover — top seal alone fails on side intakes

content.heading: Still Gaps at Corners?
content.body: Remeasure outside width and depth — pad dimensions are smaller than the cabinet. Wrong draft type with correct size still leaks.

title: Swamp Cooler Cover Size Chart & Measuring Guide
excerpt: Find the right swamp cooler cover size: measure outside width × depth × height, check common 34-inch and 40-inch fits, and size up between rows.

content.heading: Common Swamp Cooler Cover Sizes
content.body: These are shopping references, not a substitute for measuring your unit. Manufacturers list dimensions in different orders, so confirm the label is width × depth × height before ordering.

rows: Verify duct curb and top hardware
Confirm straps reach below the cabinet

content.heading: Problem: Chart Size Almost Fits
content.body: Stock charts list outside dimension ranges. Landing between two rows is common — especially when casters add height the chart does not show. Ordering down saves money once; reordering after a failed fit costs a season.

content.heading: Solution: Size Up, Then Adjust Hem
bullets: Measure outside W×D×H at widest points — casters included
Between rows → pick the next size up; drawcord or strap takes up slack
Hem should sit below the lowest louver, not above casters
Still tight at hose ports → custom pattern, not the next stock size

content.heading: When Stock Will Not Work
bullets: Rear hose panel sticks out past cabinet depth
Three models in one yard — no single chart row fits all
Control panel on the face breaks a flat rectangle

title: Swamp Cooler Covers: Sizes, Types & Winter Fit
excerpt: Choose the right swamp cooler cover by unit type, outside dimensions, winter exposure, material, and tie-down style—without leaving intake gaps.
canonicalNote: Regional search term for evaporative cooler — same product category as /blog/evaporative-cooler-covers-guide.

content.heading: Choose a Swamp Cooler Cover in 3 Steps
content.body: Measure the cabinet first, identify the airflow layout, then choose fabric for the storage season. A correct cover closes the intakes without trapping water inside the cooler.
bullets: Measure maximum width × depth × height, including casters and protrusions
Match side-draft, down-draft, rooftop, window, or portable profile
Use solid water-resistant fabric for winter; use mesh only for dry-season dust control

content.heading: Same Machine — Regional Name
content.body: "Swamp cooler" is Southwest slang for evaporative cooler. Same protection rules apply. Articles here focus on portable wheeled units in equipment yards — casters, mixed fleets, and open storage.

content.heading: Match Your Problem to an Article
bullets: Between size chart rows or casters don't fit → swamp cooler cover sizes
Side louvers still exposed after covering → side draft covers
Rain pools on top, top intake not sealed → down draft covers
Condensation in a freezing yard after proper drain/dry → insulated options
Dust on idle summer units, not winter shutdown → mesh only

title: Troubleshooting Cooler Cover Issues
excerpt: Cover blew off, holds water, smells like mold, or gaps at corners — match the symptom to a fix before you reorder the wrong size or type.

content.heading: Symptom → Cause → Fix
content.body: Work top to bottom. If the fix does not match, remeasure before reordering.

rows: Hem riding up over casters; no tie-downs
Route hem below casters; add ratchet straps to anchors
Re-tension straps to crown top; confirm down-draft cover on top-intake unit
Drain/dry fully next season before cover; clean pan now
Cover too small or wrong draft type
Remeasure outside W×D×H; match side vs down draft
Cover too small — stretched over hardware
Size up or go custom for port protrusions

content.heading: Still Stuck?
content.body: Send photos of the installed cover — hem position, tie-downs, and any gaps — with outside dimensions. Most reorder issues are sizing or draft type, not fabric quality.

title: UV Protection for Cooler Covers
excerpt: Cover faded and tore at the hem in one season? Southwest sun destroys low-denier fabric — specify 600D+ with UV-stabilized coating and expect shorter life on exposed rooftops.

content.heading: Problem: One-Season Fabric Failure
content.body: High-desert UV breaks down cheap polyester fast — especially at hem contact points and anywhere the fabric rubs on casters or roof curbs. Fading is the visible sign; brittleness and tearing at stress points follow in the same season.

content.heading: Solution: Spec for UV Exposure
bullets: 600D or higher polyester with UV-stabilized PU or vinyl coating
Darker colors fade slower than light colors on exposed sites
Rooftop and open yard storage → shortest lifespan; inspect hems yearly
Store folded in shade between seasons when possible

content.heading: When to Replace vs Repair
content.body: Small hem fraying on an otherwise sound cover → repair tape or patch. Widespread brittleness or coating breakdown → replace — UV damage is through the fabric, not just the surface.

title: Vented vs Closed Cooler Covers
excerpt: Still cold indoors with a cover on, or pads got wet under a "breathable" cover in winter? Mesh and vented fabrics are for in-season idle only — winter needs solid closure.

content.heading: Problem: Wrong Closure for the Season
content.body: Mesh keeps dust off idle summer units while air flows. Used at winter shutdown, cold outdoor air passes straight through — drafts continue and rain soaks pads. Teams sometimes pick mesh because it is lighter and cheaper; the failure shows up as cold rooms and wet pads in spring.

content.heading: Solution: Closed for Shutdown, Vented for Idle
bullets: Closed solid fabric — after full drain/dry shutdown; blocks drafts, rain, and pests
Mesh / vented — idle unit during cooling season in dusty yards; not winter
At shutdown: swap mesh for solid cover — do not leave mesh on through winter

content.heading: Interior Duct Still Drafting?
content.body: A solid cover seals outdoor intakes only. If rooms stay cold, check the interior duct damper or panel inside the house — cover fabric cannot fix an open duct path.

title: Waterproof vs Water-Resistant Cooler Covers
excerpt: Water inside the cabinet after a storm? PU-coated polyester sheds rain but stitched seams wick under standing water — vinyl is required when puddles form on top.

content.heading: Problem: Dry Climate Fabric, Wet Climate Install
content.body: 600D PU polyester is the right default for dry Southwest winters — light rain beads off. On a rooftop where water pools after storms, or in coastal exposure, prolonged standing water wicks through stitched seams. Interior rust follows even when the cover "looks fine" from the ground.

content.heading: Solution: Match to Worst Case, Not Average
bullets: Water-resistant (600D PU) — dry climates, wall mounts, light rain only
Waterproof (vinyl-coated) — rooftop ponding, heavy snow load, coastal rain
If you see puddles on top after storms → upgrade to vinyl regardless of climate zone

content.heading: Also Fix Drainage
content.body: Wrong fabric is not the only cause of interior wet — a sagging top pools water even on vinyl. Crown the top with strap tension so runoff reaches edges.

title: What Is an Evaporative Cooler Cover?
excerpt: Open intakes let cold air, rain, and pests in all winter. A cover seals the cabinet from the outside — but only after you drain and dry the unit.

content.heading: Problem: Open Intakes All Winter
content.body: Evaporative coolers need large intake panels to pull air through wet pads in summer. When the unit is off, those same openings become a straight path for cold outdoor air, rain, dust, and nesting pests. A tarp thrown over the top usually leaves side gaps — a fitted cover wraps the outside cabinet and closes every intake path.

content.heading: Solution: Match Cover Profile to Your Unit
content.body: Wrong type = gaps even when the size looks close. Identify your cooler first.
bullets: Side draft — tall cover; side louvers must be fully wrapped
Down draft — wide, low profile; top deck is the intake to seal
Rooftop — reinforced top + tie-downs; water must drain off, not into the curb
Window — frame-width fit; blocks the window opening from drafting

content.heading: Common Mistakes
bullets: Running the cooler with the cover on → overheating and motor damage
Covering a unit that still has water in the pan → rust and mold under the fabric
Using a down-draft cover on a side-draft unit → side intakes stay open

title: Winterizing Your Evaporative Cooler
excerpt: Mold smell in spring or a cracked water line? You skipped shutdown steps. Drain, dry, seal the interior duct — then install the cover last.

content.heading: Problem: Covering Too Early or While Wet
content.body: A cover on a wet unit traps moisture → rust, mold, and pad rot by spring. Shut down when nights stay below ~50°F and you will not need cooling again until spring. The cover is the last step, not a substitute for draining.

content.heading: Solution: Shutdown Checklist
content.body: Do these in order. Cleaning detail and storage tips are in the maintenance guide.
bullets: Power off at the disconnect — not just the wall switch
Close the water valve; disconnect and blow out the feed line
Drain the pan completely; leave the drain plug open
Scrub the pan; inspect pads — replace damaged ones or dry fully before covering
Seal the interior duct opening inside the house (damper or insulated panel)
Install cover — correct draft type, hem below lowest louver, tie-downs if exposed

content.heading: If You Already Have These Symptoms
bullets: Mold smell when you remove the cover → unit was wet; drain and dry fully next season
Cracked feed line in spring → line was still full of water when it froze
Still cold indoors → interior duct not sealed — cover alone does not fix in-house draft
Cover on the ground after a storm → add tie-downs; see installation guide
